summary:
Scarcast is an interactive web application that helps disaster risk reduction officers explore satellite evidence of surface change. Our case study follows Mount Balikabok, Philippines, around the reported 30 August 2026 landslide, connecting NISAR radar observations with optical imagery, terrain-derived waterways, rainfall records, and downstream impact reports.

Users can move through actual acquisition dates, inspect radar coherence and backscatter changes, select change areas, and check whether independent optical imagery also shows vegetation loss. Scarcast keeps dates, sources, and uncertainty visible so users can distinguish satellite observations from reported impacts. The goal is to make complex radar data easier to investigate and communicate when deciding where further review or field validation is needed.
details:
Scarcast helps people investigate surface change using NISAR radar data alongside optical imagery, terrain, rainfall records, and community reports. Built for the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, it is designed to help disaster risk reduction officers explore satellite evidence and identify areas that need further investigation.

Our case study focuses on Mount Balikabok, Philippines, around the reported 30 August 2026 landslide. We ask three practical questions: Where did the landscape change? What evidence supports that interpretation? What is known about the communities downstream?

What the application does

Users begin on a world map and select a study location. The dashboard organizes the investigation into three views:

  • Radar: Explore NISAR coherence, backscatter, and backscatter changes across actual acquisition dates. Select individual change patches to inspect their area, source observations, and supporting evidence.
  • Optical: Examine dated satellite imagery and an independent vegetation-change comparison. Distinguish areas with vegetation-loss support, areas without that support, and areas where clouds or invalid pixels prevent assessment.
  • Context: Connect the observations to terrain-derived waterways, reported downstream communities, rainfall totals, and a sourced event timeline. A 3D terrain view provides another way to examine the landscape.

A continuous timeline lets users move between satellite observations. Intermediate positions visually blend acquired images without generating new measurements. Users can also export a preliminary evidence brief for a selected change patch.

How it works

We use asf_search to discover NISAR products and earthaccess for Earthdata authentication and file access. Our offline processing pipeline extracts the study area and prepares georeferenced radar rasters, quality masks, metadata, and selectable change patches.

The radar-change screen is checked against an independent vegetation-change analysis derived from HLS S30 Sentinel-2 imagery. NASADEM historical elevation supplies terrain and drainage context. Published reports provide rainfall observations, event chronology, and reported community impacts.

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Leaflet, with Three.js for terrain visualization. Python and JavaScript scripts handle data preparation and evidence processing.

Our approach

Scarcast connects change observed on a mountain with the surrounding landscape and communities downstream. Users can inspect the radar signal, check independent imagery, and read relevant reports in the same workspace, with each source and acquisition date identifiable.

The design supports a sequence of questions an officer might ask: locate a change, inspect its evidence, examine nearby waterways and communities, and record what needs further checking.

Evidence and limitations

We considered acquisition timing, cloud cover, missing data, spatial resolution, and the limits of each measurement:

  • Radar change can reflect vegetation, moisture, or land-use changes as well as landslides.
  • Optical agreement does not establish the cause or exact timing of a change.
  • Terrain-derived waterways provide drainage context; they do not simulate debris movement or predict flooding.
  • Community pins are approximate reference locations, not measured flood boundaries.

Scarcast keeps these distinctions visible so users can separate satellite observations from reported impacts.

Intended impact and next steps

The current prototype supports retrospective investigation and communication. Our goal is to help local officers identify questions for further review, prepare evidence for field validation, and explain what the available observations do and do not establish.

Next steps include faster processing, additional study locations, and evaluation with disaster risk reduction officers.

AI Use Declaration

We used OpenAI Codex to assist with code development, debugging, interface revisions, documentation, and submission writing.

The satellite observations and published reports come from the cited sources. AI-assisted code processes and displays these inputs; AI did not generate the underlying satellite measurements.
